Let

\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{100}2^{-\lfloor 101k/j\rfloor }.
\]

Use

\[
2^{-m}=\sum_{n=m+1}^{\infty}2^{-n}\qquad (m\ge 1).
\]

Since all terms are nonnegative, we may interchange sums:

\[
S=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{-n}
\#\left\{(k,j):1\le j\le 100,\ k\ge1,\ \left\lfloor \frac{101k}{j}\right\rfloor\le n-1\right\}.
\]

For fixed \(j\) and \(n\),

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{101k}{j}\right\rfloor\le n-1
\iff \frac{101k}{j}<n
\iff k<\frac{jn}{101}.
\]

The number of positive integers \(k\) satisfying this is

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{jn-1}{101}\right\rfloor.
\]

Thus

\[
S=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^n}\sum_{j=1}^{100}\left\lfloor\frac{jn-1}{101}\right\rfloor.
\]

Let

\[
A_n=\sum_{j=1}^{100}\left\lfloor\frac{jn-1}{101}\right\rfloor.
\]

Since \(101\) is prime, the residues of \(j n-1\pmod{101}\) are:

- if \(101\nmid n\), they are \(0,1,\dots,99\), summing to \(4950\);
- if \(101\mid n\), they are all \(100\), summing to \(10000\).

Also,

\[
\sum_{j=1}^{100}(jn-1)=n\cdot \frac{100\cdot101}{2}-100=5050n-100.
\]

Therefore

\[
A_n=
\begin{cases}
\frac{5050n-100-4950}{101}=50(n-1),&101\nmid n,\\[2mm]
\frac{5050n-100-10000}{101}=50n-100,&101\mid n.
\end{cases}
\]

So

\[
A_n=50(n-1)-50\mathbf 1_{101\mid n}.
\]

Hence

\[
S=50\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n-1}{2^n}
-50\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-101m}.
\]

Now

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n-1}{2^n}=1
\]

and

\[
\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-101m}
=\frac{2^{-101}}{1-2^{-101}}
=\frac{1}{2^{101}-1}.
\]

Thus

\[
S=50-\frac{50}{2^{101}-1}
=\frac{50(2^{101}-2)}{2^{101}-1}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{50(2^{101}-2)}{2^{101}-1}}
\]
